transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jamal (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Aisha (NovaEdge SRE), Ben (NovaEdge ML Eng), Lara (NovaEdge CTO)
Shared artifacts referenced: deck: https://redwood.ai/decks/gpu-profiling-deepdive.pdf, benchmark spreadsheet: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/novaedge-profiles.xlsx

[00:00] Jamal: hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. this is the deep dive we scoped - kernel selection, trt-llm vs vllm, and using cuda graphs to remove launch overheads. is the agenda good?
[00:06] Lara: yes that looks great. main ask from our side is predictable p99 latency for 4k and 8k sequences, and tight cost estimates.
[00:12] Priya: perfect. quick intro from our side - i'm priya, i'll drive the profiling pieces, i'll share our trace interpretation and proposed kernel/layout changes. jamal will cover contract/pilot next steps.
[00:19] Ben: quick note, our production traffic is 70% short queries (<512) but we have a heavy tail of about 8% that are 4k-8k; those are our main pain point.
[00:27] Aisha: and we run in a VPC with private egress, currently evaluating private/on-prem options for data residency.

Summary/Goal (auto): evaluate runtime tradeoffs for NovaEdge workload and agree next steps to run a pilot and kernel-level tests.

[00:40] Priya: ok jumping in - first slide, high level: kernel selection matters a lot as sequence length grows. small seqs favor fused kernels with minimal mem-movement; long seqs amplify KV cache memory patterns and reduce benefits of certain fusions. we typically look at three levers: kernel type (fused vs modular), numeric precision (fp16 vs int8/quant), and execution pattern (static shapes with cudagraphs vs dynamic scheduling like vLLM).
[01:05] Ben: i'm curious - you mentioned fused kernels, is that the trt-llm path? i always conflate trt-llm and tensorrt custom kernels.
[01:11] Priya: good callout. trt-llm provides fused transformer kernels optimized for tensorrt graph execution (great for static/padded batches). vLLM/transformer-runtime approaches like our vllm path use streaming-friendly modular kernels (flash attention, split qkv) that are better for dynamic batching and variable seq lengths. side note: naming in transcripts sometimes flips, so trt-llm might show up as trt-llm or tensorrt-llm in docs.
[01:35] Lara: so for our mixed traffic which has both short and long tails, is there a single golden path? or do we need routing?
[01:41] Priya: routing is usually the practical answer. smart routing by sequence length or SLA can route low-latency short seqs to a fused trt-llm cluster and long tails to a vLLM-optimized cluster where KV cache and memory management is more flexible. Redwood supports automated routing policies and fallback when capacity is constrained.

[02:05] Jamal: quick business note - we can set up dedicated pools per routing tier for the pilot, keeps isolation and predictable throughput.

[02:15] Priya: demoing some traces - here's a 512 vs 8k run sample from our internal profiler (see spreadsheet). timestamped events: kernel-launch, memcpy H2D/D2H, cuBLAS gemm, flash-attention, multihead-fused, kv-insert/evict. notice for 8k the dominant time is KV management and fragmented GEMM shapes causing lower util.
[02:40] Ben: can you explain fragmented GEMM shapes?
[02:42] Priya: yeah - as seq grows, per-token matmuls change shape (batch x seq x head dims) and if you use many small dispatches you lose kernel efficiency; fused kernels collapse ops so you get one big GEMM, but that requires padded/static shapes and enough memory to hold the pad. vLLM approach keeps shapes dynamic and can stream kv per token which lowers peak mem but increases per-step kernel launches - that's where cuda graphs help.

[03:10] Aisha: we are worried about warm-up and cold-start penalties for our bursty inference. does cudagraphs really help there?
[03:15] Priya: cudagraphs are great to eliminate repeated kernel launch overhead. if your workload has repeated execution patterns (same shape, same sequence of kernels), you can capture and replay the graph which removes CPU/GPU launch overhead and reduces jitter. the caveat: cudagraphs like static sequences - changes in shape require re-capturing. for NovaEdge with mixed traffic we can capture multiple graphs keyed by sequence bucket (e.g., <=512, 513-2048, >2048) and replay based on routing.

[03:46] Ben: any numbers on win?
[03:48] Priya: from our internal tests on A100: for 512 tokens, cudagraph capture gives ~5-10% latency improvement; for 8k sequences the improvement is bigger on p99 avg because you reduce CPU-side overheads - 15-25% on p99 in some cases. throughput improves marginally because you reduce wasted CPU cycles.

[04:10] Lara: what about quantization - we'd love int8 cost reduction but worried about hallucination/regression on chat models.
[04:17] Priya: totally. we recommend a two-track approach: run int8 post-training quant (PTQ) on non-critical models first and run eval suites; Redwood Optimize provides quality monitors to compare logits and downstream evals. for many instruction-tuned models we see acceptable quality with int8 for embeddings and many generation tasks, but for instruction-sensitive outputs we may recommend fp16. also keep fallback rules - route to fp16 if quality drift detected.

[04:46] Aisha: in your experience does int8 change kernel choices?
[04:49] Priya: yes - int8 paths often use TensorRT fast kernels with specialized GEMM and reordering; some open-source runtimes lack robust int8 kernels. so if you plan int8, trt-llm/TensorRT path is usually better. but again you trade off flexibility for static-graph speed.

[05:06] [05:06] Ben: (murmur) also have custom ops for our retrieval fusion; is that painful across kernels?
[05:10] Priya: custom ops add friction: need to ensure they are captured in the cudagraph or available as device functions. we typically recommend wrapping custom ops as stable CUDA kernels and testing capture. sometimes we fall back to a tiny CPU step between graph segments, but that costs you overhead.

[05:30] Priya: moving on, kernel selection details: flash-attention (fused attention) vs cuDNN/cuBLAS GEMMs + custom attention. flash attention reduces memory movement and can be both faster and less memory hungry, but requires support in the runtime and may be sensitive to head dims. fused multihead attention in TRT-LLM is extremely fast for padded dense batches.

[05:58] Aisha: we use 40GB A100s. memory fragmentation has been a real issue when we do rolling upgrades with mixed workloads. any tips?
[06:05] Priya: memory fragmentation often stems from dynamic alloc/free patterns and mixed allocator behavior. we recommend preallocating workspace pools per worker and using memory arenas to reuse allocations. also ensure KV cache backing uses large contiguous allocations where possible - that helps cudagraphs and reduces fragmentation. Redwood's private runtime supports configurable allocators for on-prem.

[06:30] Ben: what about batch sizing and latency tradeoff?

[06:33] Priya: small batches -> lower latency but low GPU utilization; large batches -> high throughput but higher tail latency. use adaptive batching where you have a fast-path for p50 (small batches) and a batched path for high throughput. our runtime can do continuous batching with SLO-aware triggers so we can keep p95 under target while increasing throughput. also if you have priority traffic (web UI), mark it high priority to bypass batching.

[07:05] Priya: i'm showing a live flamegraph snippet - you can see kernel hotspots: GEMM kernels, flash-attention, and an expensive kv-serialize step that occurs at the end of generation. that kv step is effectively memcpy+index updates; for long sequences that becomes a big chunk.

[07:25] Ben: is that kv serialize coming from our prefix caching?
[07:27] Priya: yep, or from the way kv is stored. if you store kv in small fragments you pay linear serialization cost. we recommend chunked contiguous storage and incremental flushes, or leveraging shared GPU memory-backed KV stores so you avoid host copies.

[07:45] Lara: for VPC/on-prem, does Redwood's private runtime support HSM/KMS integration? we need KMS for key management and audit logs.

[07:50] Jamal: yes - Private includes KMS/HSM integrations, SSO/SAML, audit logs and can be deployed in VPC or air-gapped on-prem. we shared compliance docs earlier; i'll follow up with a checklist.

[08:02] Priya: jumping into trt-llm vs vLLM head-to-head: trt-llm advantages: highly optimized fused kernels, strong int8 support, cudagraph-friendly. disadvantages: less flexible for dynamic batching and streaming; captures aren't great for unpredictable shapes. vLLM advantages: dynamic scheduling, stream-first, great for low-memory streaming use cases; disadvantages: more kernel launches unless you apply cudagraphs or other batching.

[08:33] Ben: any hybrid approaches?
[08:34] Priya: yes - hybrid routing. we run a small fleet of trt-llm static nodes for predictable low-latency short seqs and a vLLM fleet for long-tail streaming. The routing layer (which Redwood supports) does sequence-length bucketing and SLA-based selection. one can even do model variant fallbacks - use quantized model on trt cluster and fp16 on vLLM cluster and fall back if quality thresholds fail.

[08:58] [08:58] Aisha: there's a lot of nuance. what are the concrete steps for the pilot?

[09:02] Jamal: proposed pilot: 2-week run. Step one: NovaEdge provides sample traffic + histograms. Step two: Redwood runs three configs in our lab and on your VPC: trt-llm int8, vLLM fp16 with cudagraph capture, and hybrid routing. Step three: compare p50/p95/p99 and cost. Step four: we do a short on-prem smoke if you want full-private.

[09:28] Priya: technical notes about profiling: we capture nvprof-level traces, cupti metrics, and our own kernel timeline. in addition we capture cuda graphs and record replay statistics. Attached in spreadsheet are columns for "kernel", "duration_ms", "stream", "bytes_moved".

[09:45] Ben: can you share an example of a kernel entry so our infra team knows what to look for?

[09:49] Priya: sure - example line: MHA_fused_forward_v2, 12.4ms, stream:1, alloc: 24MB, type: fp16. also we mark whether kernel was executed inside a cudagraph replay.

[10:00] Aisha: are there gotchas with cudagraphs and multi-stream workloads?

[10:03] Priya: yes - cudagraphs capture a sequence on a given stream. if you use multiple streams for overlap, you need to capture coordinated graphs or serialize points that sync streams. it's doable but adds complexity; we normally pick a primary stream for main computation and overlap with async memcpy streams carefully. also watch out for cudaGraphInstantiate overheads if you recreate graphs often.

[10:30] Ben: storage of KV cache — do you keep it in GPU memory persistent across requests?

[10:33] Priya: we persist per-session KV in GPU memory for active sessions; for cold sessions we page to CPU or NVMe depending on your policy. for NovaEdge with long sessions we recommend cold-evict thresholds and a persistent GPU-resident hot set. that reduces latency at the expense of reserved memory.

[10:55] Lara: any thoughts on NUMA/placement issues on multi-GPU hosts?

[10:58] Priya: very important. ensure NVLink topology and process local GPU binding are respected, colocate batch shards on GPUs with fast interconnect. also set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES carefully for pinned workers. fragmentation of PCIe vs NVLink paths can cause surprising cross-GPU memcpy bottlenecks.

[11:25] (short pause, background keyboard clicks)

[11:34] Priya: here's an example test we ran — model: small instruction-tuned LLM, batch=4 -> trt-llm int8 p99: 420ms for 512 tokens; vLLM fp16 p99: 480ms (higher) but vLLM steady throughput at 8k is 30% better due to streaming. with cudagraphs enabled, vLLM p99 dropped to 360ms in one capture scenario. corner cases apply.

[12:02] Ben: interesting, so cudagraphs can change the ordering. does Redwood keep a library of graphs per model variant?

[12:07] Priya: we do. we version graphs per model+config and reuse across deployments where shapes match. we also keep telemetry on replay success and re-capture if we see shape drift.

[12:20] Aisha: security — when you run in our VPC, do you need extra permissions to capture traces? cupti or nvprof access could be sensitive.

[12:28] Jamal: we ask for read-only access to CUDA profiling interfaces in the guest runtime; for private/on-prem we run an agent that only sends aggregated traces back or shares them via S3 in your account. we can also do fully air-gapped offline analysis if needed.

[12:45] Priya: another gotcha: cudagraph replay sometimes masks memory growth bugs because you always replay same allocations; make sure to run long-lived tests that exercise allocations to surface leaks.

[13:00] Ben: what about autoscaling? does trt-llm cluster scale differently than vLLM?

[13:04] Priya: scaling is similar but tuning differs: trt-llm nodes are capacity-bound (need more memory to pad sequences), so scale by heavy-instance counts. vLLM nodes scale by concurrency and scheduler throughput. Redwood Dedicated autoscaling supports both policies and burst capacity.

[13:25] Lara: ok can you recap the recommended initial config for our pilot?

[13:28] Priya: yes: 1) run hybrid: small trt-llm fleet with int8 for short seqs; 2) vLLM fp16 fleet for long-tail and streaming with cudagraph captures for three size-buckets; 3) set KV hotset policy to keep active sessions GPU-resident; 4) enable Redwood Optimize suggestions for batching thresholds; 5) run quality monitors for int8 fallbacks.

[13:55] Jamal: i'll send a one-pager with costs for each fleet configuration and pilot agreement.

[14:00] (brief cross talk)

[14:08] Ben: small nit - do you have an estimate of engineering effort to integrate our custom retrieval op into cudagraph capture?

[14:12] Priya: usually 2-3 engineer days to wrap op and validate capture on a standard lab env, 4-5 days if there are bespoke memory semantics. we can include that as part of the pilot scope.

[14:25] Aisha: any last security/privacy notes?

[14:28] Jamal: we support SOC2, SSO, RBAC, KMS integration, and can run in your VPC with no egress if required. I'll drop the compliance pack.

[14:36] Priya: ok final technical notes — we'll need your seq length histogram, sample prompt set (anonymized), and any custom ops. we'll run the three configs and provide kernel-level timelines, cudagraphs replay stats, and a recommendation.

[14:50] Lara: sounds good. wrap up?

[14:52] Jamal: recap of next steps — priya will run lab reproductions and share spreadsheet; aisha will provide traffic samples; i'll send pricing and pilot contract. we'll aim for follow-up week of 2026-12-14 to show results.

[14:58] Ben: thanks all.

[15:00] (call ends)
